title: TB0-01120
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXX XXXX, (principal claimant), XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX, (the minor claimants), seek protection in Canada pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

This is a hearing de novo of their claims, which, pursuant to Rule 55(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules, were heard jointly. Also, pursuant to IRPA section 167(2), the principal claimant was designated the representative for the other three claimants, who are all minors.

At the time the hearing was scheduled, XXXX XXXX was detained at the Roy McMurty Youth Centre in Brampton. While the Division alerted the Minister to a possible exclusion issue arising from his detention, the Minister did not participate in the hearing.

Originally, these claims were joined with that of XXXX XXXX, the husband of the principal claimant. XXXX XXXX is the father of the minor claimants, and all of the claimants rely, in part, on his narrative, as amended.2 XXXX XXXX claim was disjoined at the hearing of January 31, 2012. It was at this hearing that the principal claimant was designated the representative of the minor claimants. XXXX XXXX claim was then heard separately, and a negative decision was rendered. On April 26, 2012, the Federal Court refused his application for leave to have the Board's decision judicially reviewed. The principal claimant's husband has since returned to Hungary.
The principal claimant married XXXX XXXX in 2007.

In his narrative, the principal claimant's husband stated, that the claimants left Hungary because they were concerned about the welfare of the minor claimants. He described several discriminatory incidents, including an attack during which he was beaten with a baseball bat. His right shoulder was dislocated. In a second attack, he, the principal claimant and his "grandson" were attacked and he, XXXX XXXX, was beaten. In his amendment to the PIF, the principal claimant's husband described being refused promised employment at a bakery, when he turned up to sign the contract. He also described an incident on a streetcar during which three "guardsmen" spit on their daughter. When the family got off the streetcar, the guardsmen followed them. They beat them, and threatened to kill them were they to report the incident to the police. The incident ended when two passersby assisted the claimants. Amendment to the Narrative

The principal claimant filed a further amendment to the narrative.3 In her amendment, she added that her spouse was removed from Canada following his failed claim, and that he now lives in a shelter in Budapest. She stated that he is forced to live in a shelter because, being Roma, he is unable to find work, and so is unable to find shelter of his own. Their own home in XXXX is not in a habitable condition, and the principal claimant's husband does not have the money either to repair or to rebuild it. He has been attacked by racists at least once, and suffered a cut finger during the incident. The principal claimant did not know if her husband had filed a police report regarding the incident, but noted that the Federal Court has recognised that the police are known not to respond well to complaints by Roma persons.

Also, in her amendment, the principal claimant claimed that when the family lived in Budapest, she was not able to register their youngest child in daycare because the landlord would not give them the document they needed to establish that they were residents of Budapest.

The principal claimant also set out the possible effect returning to Hungary would have on the minor claimants. She alleged they would be put back to the grades they were in when they left Hungary, and their education would be adversely affected. The principal claimant also stated, that her son XXXX has been negatively affected by his father's absence. His conduct has attracted the involvement of police and the Children's Aid Society. She claimed that all of the minors would have better prospects for life in Canada than they would in Hungary. ANALYSIS Issues
The determinative issues in the claim are credibility and state protection. Credibility

The panel is aware of the principle that when a claimant swears to the truth of certain statements, this creates a presumption that they are true, unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. In other words, a claimant's sworn testimony gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of truthfulness.4 The principal claimant provided the oral testimony at the hearing. Overall, the panel found that she lacked credibility; unless she was responding to a leading question, her responses tended to be general.

The previous hearing of the claim found that the principal claimant had established the Roma ethnicity of the family, and the panel accepts that finding. However, the panel had concerns about aspects of her testimony regarding that ethnicity. The claimant's mother is white; her father was Roma. She testified that in Hungary, she is readily recognised as Roma by her manner of dress, speech and expression. To test this assertion, the panel asked the interpreter whether he perceived any differences in the principal claimant's speech. He responded that she used the same Hungarian words, but that he had some difficulty understanding her because of her grammar.

Counsel for the claimant asked the interpreter whether he had observed any differences in her pronunciation and speech pattern, to which the interpreter responded, there were none. For its part, the panel is not persuaded by the principal claimant's assertions that the way she spoke and use of language was typically Roma. Given that her mother is a white Hungarian, and also given that she was raised by her mother, the panel finds that it was equally likely that the principal claimant would speak like a white Hungarian. The panel infers, that her claims were no more than exaggerations, and while not definitive of her credibility, were indicative of her willingness to mislead the panel.

The panel asked the principal claimant why the family came to Canada. She responded, that they left Hungary because they were humiliated, given scant respect, unemployed and oppressed because of their Roma ethnicity. She described some of the experiences that led to the decision to leave. For herself, she claimed that racism and discrimination led to her having limited formal education. She left school at the end of Grade 8 because of bullying, and a lack of "moral strength to continue."

As the principal claimant started school at around age 6, after eight grades, she would have been around fifteen years old when she left school. Her first child, XXXX, was born in XXXX 2001. This means, that the principal claimant would have become pregnant in the summer of 2000, which ties in with when the then fifteen year old principal claimant would have stopped school. The panel finds that there was valid reason to doubt, and to reject, the principal claimant's stated reason for leaving school.

At the Port of Entry (POE), the principal claimant stated that she was afraid of the Hungarian Guard. She went on to state, that she was seeking Canada's protection "because we are Roma we are outcasted [sic]. Our lifeline or opportunities are totally cut off from us. When we were on the bus my child was insulted and spat on."5 The amended narrative filed by her husband added, that the attackers had followed the family and beat them. In testimony, the principal claimant added, that the attackers demanded that her husband "give her to them".

While the panel did not put the inconsistency to the claimant, in the context of her exaggeration and half-truth alluded to earlier, it is not persuaded of the truth of the whole of her statement. Specifically, the panel is not persuaded that the black uniformed men she described had demanded that her husband give her to them as she claimed. The incident allegedly took place in broad daylight, and the panel is not persuaded that, in the unlikely event that her husband had acceded to the request, the principal claimant could have been led away unwillingly. The panel is of the view that this is another instance where she has exaggerated her experiences.

In Lubana,6 Martineau, J., noted that: Normally, the Board is entitled to conclude that an applicant is not credible because of implausibilities in his or her evidence as long as its inferences are not unreasonable and its reasons are set out in "clear and unmistakable terms": see Hilo v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1991), 130 N.R. 236 (F.C.A.); Aguebor v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1993), 160 N.R. 315 (F.C.A.) ("Aguebor"); Zhou v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1994] F.C.J. No. 1087 (QL) (C.A.); and Kanyai, supra, at para. 10. Furthermore, the Board is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality: see Shahamati v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] F.C.J. No. 415 at para. 2 (QL) (C.A.); and Aguebor, supra, at para. 4. The Board may reject uncontradicted evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole, or where inconsistencies are found in the evidence: see Akinlolu, supra, at para. 13; and Kanyai, supra, at para. 11.

Following the dicta of Martineau, J., the panel rejects the uncontradicted evidence of the principal claimant, that, the Hungarian Guard demanded that her husband give her to them during the alleged incident on the street car. The panel further finds that, if true, this is the type of incident that the principal claimant's husband would likely have included in the amendment to this narrative.

The panel also finds, that there was additional valid reason to question the credibility of the principal claimant's account of the street car incident, with respect to the involvement of the police. In response to her counsel, the principal claimant alleged that the police were present during the incident, but took no action to interfere. Instead, the police treated them as if they were the perpetrators, and not the victims. In her words, "they [the police] started to yell at us to go away". That the police were present, but unhelpful, was not mentioned in either amendment to the narrative or at the POE. In fact, the principal claimant's testimony was itself internally inconsistent, as she initially testified that she did not file a police report about the incident because she did not know the names of their attackers, and could not file a report. The panel finds that this inconsistency adds to the general untrustworthiness of the principal claimant's evidence. The Minor Claimants

Counsel for the claimants submitted, that the minor claimants were important factors in the hearing. The panel concurs. On their behalves, the principal claimant submitted that, if returned, they would have experiences similar to hers, that is, they would be marginalised and ostracised. She claims that her son, XXXX Jr., already had one such experience where he was locked in a classroom instead of being allowed out to socialise with his classmates. In testimony, she blamed this experience for, at least in part, being responsible for his later reluctance to attend school here in Toronto.

XXXX Jr. was not yet seven years old when he arrived in Canada. He appeared to have attended school for one term (semester) before he was brought to Canada. It was the principal claimant's evidence that XXXX Jr. last attended school in September 2016. She testified that for about three months he would go to school, but would not enter the classroom. He walked the hallways; he told her that he quite simply could not enter the classroom. Psychological counselling was recommended; but XXXX Jr. refused to attend. When questioned by her counsel, the principal claimant testified that XXXX Jr. had fallen in with "bad company." After being prompted further, she stated that he was adversely affected by his father's absence. She testified that "we are going to see a psychologist", but there was no objective evidence in the form or ether an appointment schedule, or report, put before the hearing.

The panel accepts that a mix of factors likely affected and accounts for XXXX Jr.'s delinquency, and that this delinquency has affected his academic achievement. However, the panel is not persuaded, that upon return to Hungary, a fifteen to sixteen year old XXXX Jr. would be placed with children in Grade 1. Nor is the panel persuaded that he would be placed in a boarding (reform) school, as claimed. As it is, he appears to have abandoned schooling here in Toronto, and the panel is not persuaded that he would resume schooling in Hungary, all things being equal.

With respect to XXXX and XXXX, the panel accepts that they will experience some dislocation as they may, or may not, be able to read or write Hungarian. However, so far as XXXX is concerned that dislocation would be no different from her experience when she was first brought to Canada, and placed in the school system here. Furthermore, the principal claimant has not put any objective evidence before the panel to establish that the children would be put in Grade 1 as she asserted. The panel finds her testimony, that she was told this by persons who had returned to Hungary, speculative at best. Therefore, without more, the panel finds that there is insufficient credible evidence to persuade it that this would be the case.

With respect to education, the panel notes to address the inequity. The Hungarian central government has taken the responsibility for education away from the municipal levels, and attributed it to the government, thus the centralization would lead to better outcome. A new school inspectorate system has also been set up and started to operate in 2015.7

Country documentary evidence further states the following: 8 ...significant governmental efforts have been made in recent years for the increased enforcement of equal opportunities in education. In addition to local programmes, programmes co-funded by the European Union (Phare, HEFOP - Human Resources Operational Programme, TÁMOP - Social Renewal Operational Programme, TIOP - Social Infrastructure Operational Programme, ROP - Regional Operational Programmes), too, have been available in the magnitude of tens of billions of forints. While integrated education is largely wide-spread on an institutional level, drop-out rates and the study results of students with multiple disadvantages have yet to improve significantly. The target groups of educational equal opportunities programmes are, in every instance, regardless of ethnicity, groups of pupils/students qualifying as pupils/students with multiple disadvantages or as disadvantaged as defined in Section 121 Point 14 of Act LXXIX of 1993 on Public Education. ... The extracurricular learning centres are a form of education opted for by children and their parents out of their own free will that is designed to assist and manage learning adjusted to the personal educational needs of participants and that serves to improve the chances of integration into the formal school system. As part of the programme, 60 alternative learning facility projects were financed in total. However, the sustainability of extra-curricular learning centres and the need for the streamlining of parallel institution development and funding forms are issues yet to be resolved.

I acknowledge that the educational system in Hungary is not without discrimination towards Roma children, and that the EU has taken steps against it with respect to improvements in this area. Nonetheless, the country evidence indicates:9 ...The ERRC also reports that between 2011 and 2016, the Hungarian Supreme Court ruled that Romani children were being unlawfully segregated in five cases, and the Equal Treatment Authority convicted two municipalities for segregation; however, the Hungarian courts did not order the desegregation of any schools (ibid.). ... Sources indicate that in May 2016, the European Commission launched infringement proceedings against Hungary due to discrimination of Roma in Hungary's school system; if Hungary fails to rectify the situation, they could be referred to the European Court of Justice, which could impose financial penalties. ...Sources indicate that in Hungary, it is mandatory for all children to start kindergarten from age 3 [footnote omitted]. However, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights notes that there are not enough kindergarten spaces for Roma children in segregated areas.

The EU Roma Integration Framework was adopted under the Hungarian Presidency of the EU in the first half of 2011. Hungary was the first to develop its National Social Inclusion Strategy according to the EU framework. According to Government declarations, ...in alignment with the EU framework of National Roma Integration Strategies up to 2020, the Government aims to determine the medium-term challenges and targets of the social and labour market integration of those living in poverty, including the Roma, as well as the necessary interventions, over a period of 10 years.10

Furthermore, the country documentary evidence states the following:11 Article 66 of the Public Education Act made the regulations concerning the enrolment of children in public schools stricter from January 1, 2007. According to the modification the schools' ability to select among students is reduced as they have to admit every child whose residence is within the school district. In those cases when the number of applicant students exceeds the number of available spaces, the schools must admit disadvantaged students first and can then use a lottery system to decide the remaining ones. The new regulation also obliged local self-governments to draw school districts in a way that the percentage of multiply disadvantaged children within each school district must not be more than 15 percent higher or lower than the ratio of multiply disadvantaged children in the whole settlement. Also, the proportion of students with multiple disadvantages among neighbouring school districts should not exceed 25 percent. Other changes made it mandatory for schools and kindergartens maintained by churches and other institutions to enrol children who reside within the settlement (up to a minimum of 25 percent of the total number of children in the school), while priority is given to children with multiple disadvantages, as defined by the integration goals. The relevance of this measure was demonstrated by the fact that the proportion of multiply disadvantaged children in church-maintained schools was less than one-tenth of that of state schools, and this tendency has even escalated after 2013, since schools were taken by the central government from the municipalities. The 2007 regulation assigned the Education Authority to evaluate the enrolment procedures of schools to monitor their compliance with the new rules. The upper limit of fines which the Authority can issue was also raised to one million HUF from 100,000 HUF, but until this date the Education Authority has only investigated cases on a few occasions and has not exploited its sanctioning power. ... Following the election in 2010 the right-wing government elaborated a concept for the renewal of both the public education and the higher education system. The legal framework of the operation of the public education institutions changed significantly according to the new Public Education Law (CXC/2011) and the National Curriculum also went through major revision. The centralisation of the school system and the increased control over the teaching processes and taught content in schools have been debated extensively and criticised by basically every relevant actor of the education sector, teacher and parent organisations, education experts, academics, opposition and even governing party politicians. The systems of school administration and financing have changed in line with the new law. The municipality maintained schools were integrated into a centralised school system, which is maintained by the state. The local governments are only responsible for the school facilities, but teachers are employed and paid directly by a public school maintainer state authority (Klebelsberg Intézményfenntartó Központ, KLIK). Most of the changes entered into force after September 2013.12

The panel concludes that the claimants' fears with respect to education are speculative, and given the preponderance of the objective evidence, there is insufficient evidence to persuade the panel that the minor claimants would have to return to Grade 1. Moreover, since the claimants have left Hungary some 8 years ago, programmes at the operational level have been put in place to foster education amongst all children. It would be up to the claimants, to take advantage of those programmes. Homelessness

The principal claimant testified that the family home in XXXX has been destroyed. There was no objective evidence of that destruction put before the panel. As the principal claimant's husband is currently in Hungary, the panel finds that this evidence could readily have been obtained. In any event, the panel is not persuaded that there is a nexus between the alleged destruction of the property, and the Convention definition, because there was no reliable evidence put before the panel about who destroyed the property, or their motive for doing so.

As well, the principal claimant's mother remains in Hungary, and there was no evidence placed before the panel that they could not live with her until such time that they could establish their own household.

This matter was returned to the Board for redetermination, because the Federal Court disagreed with the Division's state protection findings, to wit, that Hungary had taken measures to ensure that state protection was extended to its Roma citizens, and that the claimants had failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection because they had never sought to avail themselves of state protection. In her testimony, the principal claimant explained the failure to seek state protection as being understandable, in a climate where the police do not routinely protect Roma persons. She seemed to assert, that even the Federal Court had accepted the lack of police protection in its decision.

The panel finds that the true reasoning behind the decision of the Federal Court lies in its statement at paragraph 15 of the decision. The statement indicates that the Federal Court found the Board had not provided any analysis as to how it reached its conclusion that there is adequate state protection in Hungary for Roma who are victims of crime, police abuse, discrimination, or persecution. The Federal Court rejected the Board's conclusions in light of documentary evidence to the contrary. The panel does not read in the Federal Court's statement a blanket acceptance that all Roma are unable to access state protection.

In this regard, the panel finds persuasive the words of Le Blanc J. in Balogh.13 For the purposes of s. 96 of the IRPA, personal targeting or past persecution is not required in order to establish a risk. Rather, persecution can be established by examining the situation of similarly situated individuals14, and the panel finds that the Balogh decision is consistent with these principles. As explained by Justice LeBlanc at paragraph 19 of this decision:15 Moreover, while the documentary evidence of general country conditions of Roma in Hungary raises human rights concerns, the mere fact of being of Roma ethnicity in Hungary is not, in and of itself, sufficient to establish that an applicant faces more than a mere possibility of persecution upon return (Csonka v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1056, at paras 67-70 [Csonka]; Ahmad v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 808, at para 22 [Ahmad]. Both subjective fear and objective fear are components in respect of a valid claim for refugee status (Csonka, art para 3). The applicant has a burden of establishing a link between the general documentary evidence and the applicant's specific circumstances (Prophète 4 v Canada (Citizenship & Immigration), 2008 FC 331, at para 17; Jarada v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 409, at para 28; Ahmad, at para 22).

Thus, in the panel's reading of jurisprudence relating to refugee claims based on Hungarian Roma ethnicity, the panel finds that it does not support a conclusion that the general country conditions are such that all Roma in Hungary face discrimination amounting to persecution. Rather, and as conducted in this case, the panel considered the particular claimants' circumstances, in combination with the general documentary evidence, to determine whether these claimants face a risk of persecution should they return to Hungary in 2018, or in the near future.

As indicated above, the panel found the principal claimant's testimony to be fraught with inconsistencies, contradictions, and unsupported speculation, such that it is not reliable. Moreover, by her own admission, at no time did the principal claimant seek to engage the state in an effort to obtain protection. Accordingly, the panel concludes that there was insufficient credible evidence upon which to find that the claimants were, at any time, being denied any fundamental rights at the time of their departure. Moreover, the panel concludes that the claimants have not rebutted the presumption of state protection, given that they did not pursue other avenues that may have been available to them. Case Law

To rebut the presumption of state protection, a refugee claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens.16 A refugee claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate, must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is, in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.17 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police, and civil authority in place, and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.18 A refugee claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection, in a functioning democracy, by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.19 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it, does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.20

Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection, to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state. The onus is on the refugee claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.21 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.22

The refugee claimant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the refugee claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.23 In a functioning democracy, a refugee claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.24

A refugee claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken, and the refugee claimant's interactions with the authorities.25 Local failures by authorities to provide protection does not mean that the state, as a whole, fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability, or refusal, to provide protection.26 No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim. Especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place, and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.27 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.28

The panel is required to determine the state protection provided at the present time that is relevant.29 The panel's analysis of the protection available to Roma in Hungary today is such that, protection is operationally adequate based on its analysis that follows. The panel notes that regard must be given to what is actually happening, and not what the state is endeavouring to put in place.30 In this case, the panel finds the government's efforts have "actually translated into adequate state protection" at the operational level.31

The panel acknowledges that the Roma minority population in Hungary, experience discrimination in many aspects of their daily lives, and at times, violence and abuse at the hands of some racist elements in Hungary. This includes, the lack of action on the part of some police officers who also demonstrate anti-Roma sentiments. The Board's documentary package indicates that "Human rights NGOs continued to report that Roma suffered social and economic exclusion and discrimination in almost all fields of life."32 However, with the formal dissolution of the Hungarian Guards in 2013, and with the right-wing Jobbik Party re-casting itself as a more inclusive but still nationalist party, the panel is not persuaded that there is a present danger to the claimants.

The panel also notes from its reading of the documentary materials, including human rights monitoring groups, the customary annual reports that the Board references and the diverse media sources, that there are no current reports of right-wing and nationalist marches or gatherings in Hungary that are targeting, harassing, and threatening Roma. While discriminatory attitudes persist among some groups and people in Hungary today, there is no documented evidence before the panel to suggest, or to establish, that other nationalist or right-wing groups have been targeting Roma today as they were in the years leading up to the claimants' departure, or that these groups are supported by the State.

Counsel for the claimants invited the panel to extrapolate, from the present position of the European Union regarding certain aspects of Hungarian democracy that, the current situation for the claimants is worse than when they came to Canada. He cites Hungary's position toward migrants as demonstrative of its position towards Roma. With respect, the panel cannot draw such a conclusion as an inevitability, as it is not only Hungary that is opposed to the mass migration seen today. State Protection and the role of the police and other agencies

The documentary evidence indicates, that police arrest and prosecute the perpetrators of crimes, including crimes committed against Roma, and other ethnic minorities and their property. If the claimants were to be dissatisfied, with the response of the authorities to their complaints, documentary evidence noted below indicates that recourse would be available to them. For example, the Independent Police Complaints Board (IPCB) investigates violations and omissions by the police. If the claimants were to return to Hungary and encounter problems in education, employment, healthcare, housing or access to business establishments, the documentary evidence indicates that recourse would be available to them. Furthermore, the documentary evidence indicates, that there are a number of organizations and agencies that assist Hungarians of Romani ethnicity, in obtaining the appropriate services and protections from the government and the authorities. The panel emphasizes, that it has considered the effect of these programs and initiatives at the operational level, or on the ground.

Furthermore, the Hungarian authorities have taken action against the Hungarian Guard Association, and have initiated processes for banning the Civil Guard Association, on the grounds that their anti-Roma activities threaten public order.33

The RPD has further considered the copious amounts of documents submitted by the claimants, all of which include reported incidents of discrimination against the Roma. The panel has also considered the submissions by counsel. However, the RPD notes, that the government prosecutes and punishes officials who commit abuses, whether in the security services or elsewhere in the government.34

Section 10.2 of the NDP states: 2. Complaints Mechanisms According to a report on discrimination in Hungary, produced by the European Union's (EU) Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA), an independent body of the EU that provides information to member states on issues of fundamental rights and Community law [footnote omitted], [t]here is no specific complaints mechanism dealing with racist and related abuse by police officers ... the options for victims to seek redress are limited. Nevertheless, if victims are subjected to abuses of police power that meet the threshold for criminal liability, they can file a report with the competent Prosecutorial Investigation Office. Abuses of power by police that are not regarded [as] a violation of fundamental rights are examined and decided upon by the head of [the] unit at the police responsible for the staff member against whom allegations of abuse were made.[footnote omitted]35

The country documentation further states that: The Hungarian National Police has been treating the educational as well as employment opportunities of the Roma youth as high priority on both strategic and operational levels since the internal instruction No. 1/2010.HNP came into force. The country police headquarters have been making a lot of efforts to spread [police] applications in the largest possible circles so that they reach more Roma youth interested in police career. Secondary [school] application system can assure [that] supported young Roma get their high school diploma, thus increasing their employment opportunities with the police. The higher education application system provides support for [Roma] to complete their college or university studies and then to get employment within the police [footnote omitted].36

Another country document provides the following information: Sources indicate that complaints can be brought to the relevant police unit or the Independent Police Complaints Board (IPCB) (Council of Europe 30 Apr. 2014, para. 28; US 25 June 2015, 9; HHC 29 June 2015). In correspondence with the Research Directorate, a representative from the Hungarian Helsinki Committee (HHC), a civil society organization that monitors the human rights and legal situation in Hungary (HHC n.d.), stated that complaints can be submitted to the responsible police unit within 30 days of the alleged violation and that complaints can also be submitted "with the help of a legal representative" [footnote omitted]. The representative added that the complaint is decided on by the head of the relevant police unit during an "administrative procedure" (ibid.). The complainant may appeal the "first instance decision," which is decided upon by the superior of the same police unit (ibid.). If the "first instance" decision was rendered by the "National Police Chief, the head of the department responsible for internal affairs, or the head of the counter-terrorism unit, no appeal may be submitted" (ibid.). In the cases of a "first instance" decision by aforementioned department heads, or a "second instance" decision, complainants may appeal to the courts (ibid.). The same source further states that as a result of the police complaint being submitted to the police unit allegedly responsible for the incident, they "cannot be regarded as an independent forum for deciding upon the given complaint" and that this may have a negative impact on the effectiveness of "ordinary complaint procedures" [footnote omitted].37 ... 2.1 Independent Police Complaints Board (IPCB) According to sources, the IPCB is available to investigate police activity that violate fundamental rights [footnote omitted]. According to the website of the IPCB, complaints must be filed, in person or in writing, within 20 days of the incident or 20 days of the time that the individual became aware of the infringement (ibid.). If there are extenuating circumstances that can be proven, such as a lengthy hospital stay, the time limit is extended (ibid.). The same source further states that if the 20-day deadline has passed, but not 30 days, an individual can file a complaint with "the head of the police office (Police Chief) of which subordinate has taken the challenged measures against the complainant" (ibid.). The case will be forwarded by the IPCB to the relevant police organ if the board concludes that: - there was no violation of a fundamental right - the infringement of a fundamental right cannot be decided because of -the contradiction between the statement of the complainant and Police; - there was an insignificant infringement of fundamental rights. (ibid.) Sources further state that, should the Board find that a violation of fundamental rights has occurred, they submit a non-binding recommendation to the head of the National Police.38 ... 2.2 The Equal Treatment Authority According to the European Commission Against Racism and Intolerance, the Equal Treatment Authority is an independent body established by the Hungarian government "to receive and deal with individual and public complaints about unequal treatment" and it reviews the complaints it receives to establish whether the law on equal treatment has been violated, including on the basis of ethnic origin" (EU n.d.). The UN Working Group report similarly states that the Equal Treatment Authority is an independent body that was established "to protect, enforce and promote equality and the right to equal treatment by monitoring the observance" of the Equal Treatment Act [footnote omitted].39 ... According to the same source, in 2012 a "unified Ombudsman institution" was created in order to replace the old structure, which had four Ombudsmen (Hungary 11 July 2012). The "Closing and Miscellaneous Provisions" of the Fundamental Law of Hungary provide the following: 16. As of the entry into force of the Fundamental Law, the designation for the office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Citizens' Rights shall be Commissioner for Fundamental Rights. The legal successor of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Citizens' Rights, the Parliamentary Commissioner for National and Ethnic Minority Rights and the Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations shall be the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights. As of the entry into force of the Fundamental Law, the Parliamentary Commissioner for National and Ethnic Minority Rights in office shall become Deputy of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights responsible for the protection of the rights of nationalities living in Hungary; as of the entry into force of the Fundamental Law, the Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations in office shall become Deputy of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights responsible for the protection of the interests of future generations; their mandates shall terminate upon the termination of the mandate of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights. (Hungary 2011) The Commissioner's website states that anyone can submit a complaint, orally or in writing, to the Commissioner if the activity or omission of the public and/or other organs performing public duties ... infringes a fundamental right of the person submitting the petition or presents an imminent danger. When the person reporting has exhausted the available administrative legal remedies, not including the judicial review of an administrative decision, or if no legal remedy is available to him or her. (Hungary n.d.d.)40 ... 3. Resources Available for Assisting Individuals Filing a Complaint According to the UN Working Group report, there are legal aid services available to "indigent persons with legal problems, which may also include the violation of the right of equal treatment" (UN 3 July 2014, para. 76). The HHC representative stated that complainants can be represented by "human rights NGOs or foundations, minority self governments or certain law professors" and that legal aid services are available for "participation in the police complaints procedure" (HHC 29 June 2015). The same source further stated that if Legal Aid is granted, the complainant "may receive legal advice" in addition to having the legal aid provider complete the complaint submission for them (ibid.). According to the HHC website, it offers legal assistance "regarding complaints concerning detention and police measures" (ibid. n.d.). In order to process an application for legal assistance, the applicant must submit a letter that outlines their case, including: personal information, the type of case requiring assistance (i.e. police treatment), time and place of the event, the authorities involved and whether the applicant has previously received legal aid (ibid.). The same source further states that the HHC will respond, in writing, to all requests for assistance within 60 days "if possible" (ibid). Sources state that victims of hate crimes are unable to get sufficient support, including counselling and legal assistance (AI 6 Aug. 2013; Council of Europe 16 Dec. 2014, para. 85). According to the HHC representative, in 2013, seven percent of complainants involved in a complaints procedure before the IPCB had a legal representative (HHC 29 June 2015). She added that there is no data available on legal representation provided during "ordinary police complaint procedures" (ibid.).41 4. Police Response to Complaints Submitted by Roma The HHC representative stated that in Hungary, it is illegal "to record the complainants' ethnicity or perceived ethnicity" and as such, statistics are unavailable on the success rate of complaints submitted by Roma (ibid.). The UN Working Group report similarly states that there is a "lack of ...data disaggregated by ethnicity" (UN 3 July 2014, para. 121).42 4.1 Police Response to Hate Crimes According to the BBC, in Hungary "[m]any people are not familiar with the concept of hate crime - the idea that the targeting of people because of the colour of their skin, their religious belief, or their sexual orientation is different to ordinary crime." According to sources, the police in Hungary lack both the resources and awareness of the proper procedures for investigating and responding to hate crimes.43 ... According to the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe's report, police in Hungary have been given powers, in the form of new legal provisions, to counter the activities of paramilitary groups "engaging in racist violence and conducting certain activities such as patrolling areas inhabited by Roma" (Council of Europe 16 Dec. 2014, para. 81). The same source reports that a professional network has been set up among those within the national police that are responsible for "dealing with hate crimes."44 ... The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) similarly reports that in 2013, 48 hate crimes were recorded by the police, 30 were prosecuted and 14 were sentenced (OSCE n.d.).45

The RPD finds that the government has enacted legislation, and put in place many tactical initiatives across several departments and they are producing results on the ground. The RPD finds that the documentary evidence, as noted above, demonstrates that Hungary continues to provide protection for all its citizens, including Roma and other ethnic minorities. Although not perfect, the RPD finds that the evidence demonstrates that Hungary's progressively evolving measures/actions to provide protection for its citizens, including Roma, are actually having an impact operationally on the ground. The evidence also demonstrates, that police do investigate crimes against Roma, and that perpetrators are being held responsible when there is sufficient evidence.
In the final analysis, the question to be answered is if there is adequate state protection, at the operational level, for these particular claimants.

In Mudrak,46 Mr. Justice Annis states that: More substantively, suggesting that police oversight agencies have no role in demonstrating adequate state protection is like saying senior policing management has no role in policing due to their oversight function, or saying that policing is a short-term operational exercise. Similarly, denying oversight agencies an important role in police protection would suggest that the police complaints process, and thereafter the courts in Canada, have no responsibility in ensuring adequate policing. This is surely an unsustainable proposition. It is no counter-argument that Canadian police are more responsive to complaints about their conduct, which in some recent instances at least, might be challenged. The point is that the evidence in the Hungarian Roma persecution claims indicates that the oversight agencies are diligent in their investigations and in reporting their findings to the police. The transparency and accompanying public criticism of the state protection apparatus is an important ingredient to reforms and improvement in protection services accorded to Roma citizens. The requirement to access police oversight agencies is particularly important where the persecution is in the form of random incidents, such as is normally the case for members of the Roma community. Adequate state protection against random crime must operate at a community level over a longer time frame, because responding to any particular victim cannot assure that future random attacks from other assailants will not occur. To the extent that random criminal conduct can be prevented by means other than increased patrols, effective policing can have a deterrent effect by arresting and successfully prosecuting wrongdoers accompanied by the declaratory publicity attached to successful convictions. Thus, looking ahead, no crime prevention process can be effective if victims of crime do not report incidents to the police and proactively cooperate in their investigations, including complaining if not satisfied with the efforts of the police. If the rhetorical question is whether all members of the Roma community will be better protected from a rule requiring they follow up instances of inadequate policing with oversight agencies, I would argue, yes it would.

The RPD concludes, that as stated above, the burden is on the claimants to provide clear and convincing evidence that the state is either unwilling, or unable, to provide them with adequate protection. It is not for the RPD to provide that proof, rather it is the claimant who bears the legal burden, of rebutting the presumption that state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the panel, on a balance of probabilities.47
The panel concludes, after careful consideration of all of the evidence, that the claimants have not rebutted the presumption of state protection. Indeed, they made no effort to obtain it.
The panel is further guided by the recent decision X (Re) 2017 CANLII 144421 (CA CISR), in which it was determined that state protection was available to the claimants.48

The RPD is further guided by the recent Federal Court decision in which Justice Boswell found, that the RPD reasonably considered the legislative measures taken by the Hungarian government, and their operational effectiveness: The RPD reasonably concluded that the Applicants had not provided sufficient evidence either to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection in Budapest or to show that relocating to Budapest would be unreasonable in view of the Applicants' particular situation and circumstances.49 CONCLUSION

The panel concludes that state protection would be reasonably forthcoming to these claimants, in their particular situation and circumstances, if they required it and were to diligently seek it, upon return to Hungary.

The RPD concludes that in the particular circumstances of these claimants, the claimants have not established a serious possibility of persecution, or that they would, on a balance of probabilities, be personally subjected to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture upon return to Hungary.

Accordingly, these claims are rejected. (signed) "H. Ross" H.
